title: Algebra restriction for a symmetric weak approximation
statement:
Use quasicategories, coherent functors, full subcategories, equivalences and weak contractibility of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], inner and cocartesian fibrations of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations], symmetric infinity operads of [lem-coef-symmetric-operadic-fibration-recognition], and ordered join slices of [lem-cbc-relative-coslice-left-fibration], with opposite slices as in [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-equivalence]. Work in a fixed sufficiently large universe. Let $p:P\to N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)$ and $q:Q\to N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)$ be small symmetric infinity operads, let $C$ be a small quasicategory, and let $f:C\to P$ be a functor. Call an edge $u$ of $C$ $f$-inert when $f(u)$ is inert in $P$.

For a categorical fibration $g:D\to P$, meaning an inner fibration lifting equivalences with prescribed source, impose the following two conditions. First, for every $d\in D$ over $\langle n\rangle$ and every colour projection $\rho_i:\langle n\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$, there is a locally $pg$-cocartesian edge $d\to d_i$ over $\rho_i$ whose image is inert in $P$. Locally means cocartesian after pullback along that particular base edge. Second, for every $d\in D$ and edge $\alpha:x\to g(d)$ in $P$, let $B=P_{/g(d)}$, regard $\alpha$ as a vertex of $B$, and form
$$H_g(d,\alpha)=D_{/d}\times_{B}B_{\alpha/}.$$
The map $D_{/d}\to B$ is induced by $g$ and $B_{\alpha/}\to B$ evaluates the target. Let $F_g(d,\alpha)$ be its full subcategory on vertices given by $\beta:d'\to d$ and an inert edge $\gamma:x\to g(d')$, together with a coherent triangle $g(\beta)\gamma\simeq\alpha$. Require $F_g(d,\alpha)$ to be weakly contractible. All morphisms and higher simplices are those of the displayed pullback; in particular a comparison $k:d'\to d''$ need not be inert. The join slice convention is $(R_{/r})_m=\{\Delta^m\star\Delta^0\to R\text{ with last vertex }r\}$; the coslice has the fixed vertex first. These formulas specify the higher coherence data without taking only isomorphism classes.

Say that $f$ is a weak approximation if there are a small quasicategory $D$, a categorical equivalence $e:C\to D$ and a categorical fibration $g:D\to P$ satisfying the preceding two conditions, with $f=ge$. For a categorical-fibration weak approximation $g:D\to P$, let $\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$ be the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}_{N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)}(D,Q)$ on functors which carry the locally $pg$-cocartesian colour-projection edges specified in the first condition to inert edges of $Q$. Here the ambient functor simplicial set is the degreewise fibre over $pg$, retaining all coherent transformations over the base. For any witness $f=ge$ as above, restriction is an equivalence of ambient relative functor categories
$$e^*:\operatorname{Fun}_{N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)}(D,Q)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}_{N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)}(C,Q).$$
Define $\mathcal A_f(C,Q)$ to be the full replete essential image of $\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$ under this equivalence; this subcategory is independent of the witness. Full replete essential image means the full subcategory on objects equivalent to some restricted object. For $P$ itself, $\operatorname{Alg}(P,Q)$ is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}_{N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)}(P,Q)$ on functors preserving all inert edges of $P$.

If $f$ is a weak approximation and the strict colour-fibre functor $C\times_{N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)}\{\langle1\rangle\}\to P_{\langle1\rangle}$ is an equivalence of quasicategories, restriction induces an equivalence of full infinity categories
$$f^*:\operatorname{Alg}(P,Q)\longrightarrow\mathcal A_f(C,Q).$$
There is no categorical-fibration hypothesis on $f$ itself and no space hypothesis on $P_{\langle1\rangle}$. The assertion includes empty colour categories and all nullary operations.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Definition 2.3.3.6 (weak approximations for categorical fibrations and arbitrary functors), Definition 2.3.3.20 (algebras), and Theorem 2.3.3.23(1), printed pp. 260 and 266-268. Theorem 2.3.3.23(2), which assumes a Kan colour category, is not used Read online on 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical result.

proof.text: Put $S=N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)$. We first record how the chosen witness $f=ge$ can be used in strict relative functor categories. For an isofibration $V\to B$, postcomposition $\operatorname{Fun}(T,V)\to\operatorname{Fun}(T,B)$ is an isofibration by exponentiation (take the empty subobject of $T$). Precomposition by an equivalence $e:C\to D$ is an equivalence on the two total functor categories: compose with a quasi-inverse of $e$ and its two natural equivalences, which remain equivalences by the pointwise criterion. The strict fibres over the prescribed base functors are categorical pullbacks by the isofibration-pullback statement. The equivalence of these pullbacks therefore gives the asserted equivalence $e^*$ on strict relative functor categories, with all transformations. The maps $P\to S$ and $Q\to S$ are isofibrations: base isomorphisms are inert, their cocartesian lifts have inverse lifts, and cocartesian cancellation/initiality identifies the composites with identities. This argument also applies with $V\to B$ equal to either witness $D'\to P$. Consequently two witnesses admit an equivalence $k:D\to D'$ over $P$ and an equivalence $ke\simeq e'$ over $P$: obtain $k$ from the essential surjectivity of restriction, and its inverse from the other restriction; full faithfulness identifies their composites. Such an equivalence identifies the local lift categories over each fixed colour projection. By the cocartesian mapping criterion it preserves and reflects their locally cocartesian edges, and it preserves the condition that the image in $P$ is inert. Hence it identifies the two local-projection algebra subcategories. This proves the claimed independence of the witness as well as the ambient transport used below.

source.place: Definitions 2.3.3.6 and 2.3.3.20, Remark 2.3.3.7; expanded strict-fibre argument

proof.text: The unary hypothesis does pass to this witness, for a specific reason. The strict fibres $C_{\langle1\rangle}$ and $D_{\langle1\rangle}$ are quasicategories: the base is the nerve of an ordinary category, so a filler of a horn whose base is constant has constant base. For two objects of the fibre their mapping spaces are exactly the components over $1_{\langle1\rangle}$ of the ambient mapping spaces. The fully faithful equivalence $e$ identifies these components. Given $d\in D_{\langle1\rangle}$, choose $c$ and an equivalence $e(c)\simeq d$. Its base is a pointed bijection onto $\langle1\rangle$, forcing $c$ to have arity one and that bijection to be the identity. Thus $e_{\langle1\rangle}$ is also essentially surjective, and the equivalence criterion gives that it is an equivalence. Since $f_{\langle1\rangle}=g_{\langle1\rangle}e_{\langle1\rangle}$, $g_{\langle1\rangle}$ is an equivalence. All subsequent steps concern $g$, and Step 1 will return the answer to $f$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, first reduction; explicit check of the strict unary fibre

proof.text:
We will use the symmetric product axiom in its relative-cone form. For objects $z_i\in Q_{\langle1\rangle}$, the Segal equivalence produces $z\in Q_{\langle n\rangle}$ and inert projection legs to the $z_i$ (correct equivalent endpoints by the isofibration property). These legs form a $q$-limit over the discrete colour-projection cone; conversely such a relative product cone has inert legs. Here is the mapping-space verification, to specify exactly which axiom is used. For any test cone $t=(a\to a_i)$, put $M=\operatorname{Map}_Q(a,z)$, $V=\prod_i\operatorname{Map}_Q(a,z_i)$ and $H=\prod_i\operatorname{Map}_Q(a_i,z_i)$, and use subscript $S$ for their base analogues. The symmetric output-mapping axiom says on every fibre over an edge $u$ that $M\to V\times^h_{V_S}M_S$ is an equivalence; homotopy-fibre detection makes it an equivalence of spaces. The join-cone mapping formula and pullback pasting give
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(\{1,\ldots,n\}^{\triangleleft},Q)}(t,z)\simeq H\times^h_V M\simeq H\times^h_{H_S}(H_S\times^h_{V_S}M_S),$$
exactly the defining relative-limit square. For the converse, compare the proposed cone with the constructed inert cone with the same boundary and base. The same relative universal square, on its fibres over the identity base cone and identity boundary, supplies maps in both directions and contractible spaces of comparisons; their composites are identities up to homotopy. The cone vertices are therefore equivalent over $\langle n\rangle$, so the proposed legs are inert by the cocartesian mapping criterion. This includes $n=0$: the products of spaces are points and the required equivalence is $M\simeq M_S$. No presentability of $Q$ is used.

source.place: Definition 2.1.1.10 and Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, relative-product uses on pp. 267-268

proof.text:
Take the Cartesian unstraightening $u:E\to\Delta^1$ of $g:D\to P$, with $E_0=P$ and $E_1=D$. Its cross-fibre mapping spaces satisfy $\operatorname{Map}_E(x,d)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_P(x,g(d))$, naturally: this is the Cartesian mapping-fibre formula at a chosen Cartesian edge $g(d)\to d$. The colimit of the classifying diagram $D\to P$ is $P$, since its index has final object $P$. The Cartesian-colimit-localization theorem supplies a retraction $r:E\to P$ and the equivalence
$$\operatorname{Fun}(P,T)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathrm{Cart}(u)}(E,T).$$
Its canonical colimit cocone has the identity leg on the terminal object $P$ and the leg $g$ on $D$; choose this standard representative so $r|_P=1_P$ and $r|_D=g$. If the simplicial representatives record these endpoint maps only up to coherent equivalence, the exponentiation isofibration lifts the endpoint equivalences and the isofibration-pullback statement identifies the resulting strict fibres. Give $E$ the base functor $pr$. Apply this equivalence for both $T=Q$ and $T=S$; strict fibres are categorical fibres by Step 1. Let $\mathcal X$ be the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}_{S}(E,Q)$ whose restriction to $P$ preserves inert arrows and whose $u$-Cartesian arrows have equivalence images. Then restriction $\mathcal X\to\operatorname{Alg}(P,Q)$ is an equivalence, with inverse $A\mapsto Ar$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, p. 266: Cartesian cylinder, retraction and category X

proof.text: Fix $x\in P_{\langle n\rangle}$. Write $K_x=D\times_EE_{x/}$, with objects $\alpha:x\to g(d)$, and let $I_x\subset K_x$ be full on those objects for which $\alpha$ is inert in $P$. These are quasicategories, using the join-coslice left fibration and pullback along $D\to E$. Compare $K_x$ with $K'_x=D\times_PP_{x/}$, formed with $g$. The retraction $r$ of Step 4 satisfies $r|_P=1_P$ and $r|_D=g$, so it induces a map $K_x\to K'_x$ over $D$. Both are left fibrations over $D$ by the join-coslice left-fibration statement and pullback. On the fibre over $d$ the map is $\operatorname{Map}_E(x,d)\to\operatorname{Map}_P(x,g(d))$ induced by $r$. By the Cartesian mapping-fibre statement, composition with the Cartesian edge $c_d:g(d)\to d$ identifies the source with $\operatorname{Map}_P(x,g(d))$. The Cartesian-colimit localization says that $r$ carries $c_d$ to an equivalence of $P$. Hence the fibre map is an equivalence, and the vertex-fibre criterion for left fibrations makes $K_x\to K'_x$ an equivalence over $D$. Inertness of an object is read off from its image in $P$, so this equivalence identifies $I_x$ with the full subcategory $I'_x\subset K'_x$ on inert $\alpha$. It therefore identifies the homotopy comma categories $(I_x)_{/a}$ and $(I'_x)_{/r(a)}$. Steps 6 and 7 compute their indexing categories in $K'_x$ through the same equivalence. Now let $a:x\to g(d)$ be an object of $K'_x$. The comma category $(I'_x)_{/a}$ has objects $\beta:d'\to d$ and inert $\gamma:x\to g(d')$, together with the coherent triangle $g(\beta)\gamma\simeq a$. Its simplices are the simultaneous join-slice simplices of the displayed $F_g(d,a)$ from the statement, so it is weakly contractible. Hence so is $(I_x)_{/a}$ for every object $a$ of $K_x$. The opposite comma criterion says that $I_x\to K_x$ is coinitial. Its cone comparisons, applied to $Q$ and $S$, identify the constant-source mapping spaces naturally; together with the join-cone formula they preserve and reflect the relative-limit square. The dual relative-join-slice restriction supplies extensions with exactly prescribed boundary on $K_x$ and prescribed base cone. Thus both existence and the universal property of a $q$-limit over $K_x$ can be tested on $I_x$. Notice that $I_x$ is full: its comparisons were never restricted to inert arrows of $D$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, p. 267: coinitial inert-factorization subcategory

proof.text: Let $J_x\subset I_x$ be full on the objects with target in $D_{\langle1\rangle}$. Take $A_0\in\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$ and put $H=A_0|_{I_x}$. We claim $H$ is pointwise $q$-right Kan extended from $J_x$. At $\alpha:x\to g(d)$ in $I_x$, say $d$ has arity $m$, the indexing coslice $(J_x)_{\alpha/}$ splits into $m$ components indexed by the output colours of $d$. To see this, a triangle $x\to g(d)\to g(d')$ with both maps from $x$ inert and $d'$ unary forces the base map $d\to d'$ to be a unique projection $\rho_i:\langle m\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$. Cocartesian cancellation makes the edge in $P$ inert as well. Each component is the lift category of arrows $d\to d'$ over that fixed base edge, with the additional inert-composite condition. Choose the locally $pg$-cocartesian projection $\delta_i:d\to d_i$ promised by the hypothesis. Its image is inert, so its composite with $\alpha$ gives an object of the component. In the pullback over the fixed base edge, cocartesian initiality makes $\delta_i$ initial; the same is true in the full subcategory just described because it contains $\delta_i$. The join-slice mapping formula identifies these lift categories with the stated coslice components, including the contractible triangle choices. The relative-limit initial-components lemma reduces the Kan condition to the discrete cone $A_0(d)\to A_0(d_i)$. Its legs are inert by the definition of $\mathcal A_g$, so Step 3 proves the required relative product. This also handles $m=0$, when the indexing coslice is empty.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, p. 267: right Kan extension from the unary inert targets; initial, not final, lift objects

proof.text:
The category $J_x$ is the disjoint union of $n$ components $J_{x,i}$, according to the base projection $\rho_i:\langle n\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$. Choose inert projections $x\to x_i$ in $P$ and, by the equivalence $g_{\langle1\rangle}$ established in Step 2, objects $d_i$ with equivalences $x_i\simeq g(d_i)$. These give objects $t_i=(x\to g(d_i))$ in $J_{x,i}$. They are initial. Indeed for $t=(x\to g(d))$ in this component, its mapping space from $t_i$ is the homotopy fibre of
$$\operatorname{Map}_{D_{\langle1\rangle}}(d_i,d)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}^{\rho_i}_P(x,g(d))$$
over the arrow specifying $t$. The first map is an equivalence onto $\operatorname{Map}_{P_{\langle1\rangle}}(g(d_i),g(d))$ by full faithfulness, and precomposition with the inert arrow specifying $t_i$ is an equivalence by the cocartesian mapping criterion. Its fibre is contractible. The displayed mapping fibre is the join-coslice mapping formula (or the same relative cocartesian criterion), so the argument includes the coherent triangles. The initial-components lemma and Step 3 now give a $q$-limit of $A_0|_{J_x}$ over the prescribed base cone, and characterize such cones by inert legs to the $A_0(d_i)$. In arity zero $J_x$ is empty; the arity-zero axiom of $Q$ gives its relative empty product.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23(1) proof, p. 267: unary components; explicit initiality calculation

proof.text: Apply the cone-comparison clause of relative right Kan restriction to Step 6: the relative limit on $J_x$ extends to one on $I_x$, and an existing cone on $I_x$ is limiting exactly when its unary restriction is. Step 5 then extends it to $K_x$ and detects its relative universal property there. Consequently, for every $A_0\in\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$, the relative limits required to extend $A_0$ from the full subcategory $D\subset E$ exist at every vertex of $P$. At a vertex $d\in D$, the indexing category $D\times_E E_{d/}$ has initial object $1_d$, and the initial-components lemma gives its canonical limit at $A_0(d)$. Relative right Kan restriction now produces an extension $A:E\to Q$ over $S$, on all coherent simplices. More precisely, such an $A$ is right Kan extended from $A_0$ if and only if for each $x$ its legs to the chosen initial unary targets $d_i$ of Step 7 are inert. This criterion follows by applying in order Step 5, the cone comparison of Step 6, the initial-components lemma of Step 7, and the converse product criterion of Step 3.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, pp. 267-268: (a) and the precise criterion (b-prime)

proof.text: Suppose $A\in\mathcal X$. The localization equivalence of Step 4 gives $A\simeq(A|_P)r$ over $S$. Restricting to $D$ shows that $A_0=A|_D$ carries every specified local projection to an inert edge, since $g$ carries it to an inert edge and $A|_P$ preserves these. Inertness is invariant under equivalent functors by the cocartesian mapping criterion, so $A_0\in\mathcal A_g$. For each $x$, its legs to the objects $d_i$ of Step 7 are composites of inert arrows in $P$ and Cartesian comparison edges, which $A$ sends to equivalences. Their images are therefore inert. Step 8 proves that $A$ is pointwise right Kan extended from $A_0$.

Conversely, let $A$ be right Kan extended from $A_0\in\mathcal A_g$. For $d\in D_{\langle n\rangle}$ choose its local projections $d\to d_i$ and put $x=g(d)$. The objects $(x\to g(d_i))$ are among the initial unary targets of Step 7: they are inert, and the mapping-space calculation there applies to any such object. Step 8 makes the legs $A(x)\to A_0(d_i)$ inert. The legs $A_0(d)\to A_0(d_i)$ are inert by the algebra condition. They are two relative product cones with the same boundary and base; the comparison $A(x)\to A_0(d)$ induced by the Cartesian edge is therefore an equivalence by Step 3's universal-comparison calculation. All $u$-Cartesian edges have equivalence images. For the canonical Cartesian edge $g(d)\to d$ this was just proved. For any other $u$-Cartesian edge $e:x\to d$, the Cartesian mapping-fibre statement factors it through the canonical edge by an edge $h:x\to g(d)$ in $P$. Since both edges over $\Delta^1$ are Cartesian, the dual of cocartesian composition and the relative-cone equivalence shows that $h$ is Cartesian over the identity and hence an equivalence; $A$ sends both $h$ and the canonical edge to equivalences. A $u$-Cartesian edge over a degenerate edge of $\Delta^1$ is an equivalence by the same lift-category comparison with the identity, and $A$ sends it to an equivalence. Thus condition (ii) defining $\mathcal X$ holds, including at arity zero.

Next let $v:x\to y$ be inert in $P$. Choose inert colour projections $y\to y_j$, replace $y_j$ by equivalent $g(d_j)$ using $g_{\langle1\rangle}$, and use the Cartesian edges $g(d_j)\to d_j$. Step 8 makes $A(x)\to A_0(d_j)$ inert. The latter Cartesian comparisons are equivalences, so $A(x)\to A(y_j)$ is equivalent, by an inverse equivalence, to an inert composite; it is inert by cocartesian composition and the mapping criterion. Applied to $y$ itself the same reasoning makes $A(y)\to A(y_j)$ inert. To deduce that $A(v)$ is inert, take a cocartesian lift of its inert base map from $A(x)$ and factor $A(v)$ through it by the cocartesian mapping criterion. Both resulting cones to the $A(y_j)$ are relative products by Step 3; their comparison over the identity is an equivalence. Thus the factor after the chosen cocartesian lift is an equivalence, and cocartesian composition makes $A(v)$ cocartesian. This also applies when $y$ has arity zero, using the empty relative product. Therefore $A|_P$ preserves every inert arrow and $A\in\mathcal X$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23 proof, p. 268: (b), converse; explicit Cartesian-edge and all-inert tests

proof.text: By Steps 8-10, $\mathcal X$ is exactly the full subcategory of pointwise right Kan extensions whose restrictions are in $\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$. The universal-restriction theorem gives a trivial Kan fibration $\mathcal X\to\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$, because every such boundary has an extension by Step 8; pulling the theorem's restriction back to this full subcategory retains the boundary-lifting property. Combined with Step 4, this yields $g^*:\operatorname{Alg}(P,Q)\simeq\mathcal A_g(D,Q)$. Step 1 transports it through $e^*$ to $\mathcal A_f(C,Q)$. The resulting functor on an arbitrary simplex is $A\mapsto A\circ g\circ e=A\circ f$, since the section in Step 4 was composition with $r$. It is the displayed restriction functor, with all noninvertible transformations and their higher coherences. Step 1 also proved that the target is independent of the witness. If the colour categories are empty, no unary choices are needed at positive arity; the remaining arity-zero cases were covered in Steps 3, 6, 7 and 10. No Kan hypothesis on the colour category has been introduced.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.3.23(1), end of proof and restriction identification
